# Appendix: Reference and Field Notes

# Complexity at a Glance

| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Typical extra space | Stable? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Selection | n² | n² | n² | 1 | No |
| Insertion | n | n² | n² | 1 | Yes |
| Bubble (early exit) | n | n² | n² | 1 | Yes |
| Merge | n log n | n log n | n log n | n | Yes |
| Quick | n log n | n log n | n² | log n avg. recursion | Usually no |
| Heap | n log n | n log n | n log n | 1 | No |
| Counting | n+k | n+k | n+k | k or n+k | Can be |
| Radix | d(n+k) | d(n+k) | d(n+k) | implementation-dependent | depends on stable passes |
| Bucket | depends | often n under assumptions | can be n² | buckets | depends |
| Shell | gap-dependent | gap-dependent | gap-dependent | 1 | Usually no |
| Timsort | n | n log n | n log n | up to n scale | Yes |
| Introsort | n log n class* | n log n | n log n | log n-ish control | No |

`*` Production hybrids and cutoff details make a one-cell “best case” summary less informative than for elementary sorts.

# Vocabulary

**Adaptive:** benefits from existing structure/order in the input.

**Auxiliary space:** storage used in addition to the input itself.

**Comparison sort:** learns ordering primarily through pairwise comparisons.

**In-place:** uses only small/constant auxiliary storage under the conventional model.

**Invariant:** a condition guaranteed to remain true at a specified point in an algorithm.

**Inversion:** a pair of items appearing in the opposite relative order from the target order.

**Key:** the information used to determine an item's ordering position.

**Partition:** rearrange/divide data according to its relationship to a pivot or criterion.

**Stable:** preserves the original relative order of items with equal keys.

**Run:** a contiguous sequence already ordered monotonically.

# Learner Draft 0.1 Field Notes

This draft is intentionally meant to accumulate criticism.

For each chapter, mark any place where:

1. an instruction is ambiguous when cards are actually on the table;
2. the physical procedure accidentally differs from the algorithm being taught;
3. terminology arrives before its motivation;
4. an exercise is too easy, tedious, or large;
5. the computer/card comparison produces an unexpected insight worth expanding;
6. code helps or distracts;
7. a diagram would replace a paragraph;
8. the canonical deck order creates an interesting special case;
9. you discover a better physical gesture or layout;
10. you can explain the algorithm more clearly after doing it than the book explained it beforehand.

Those observations are not merely corrections. They are the raw material for the teaching edition.
